senses.label: Worth set by exchange
senses.summary: A thing is worth what it will fetch; need brings goods to exchange, and money measures them.
markers: need is what makes goods comparable in exchange

sources.note: The Lydians the first known to coin and use gold and silver money, and the first retail traders. Attests coin, market and retail; the account of need holding exchange together is first spelled out later (Aristotle).
Need holds exchange together; money as its measure.
Attributed maxim: a thing is worth what its buyer will pay.

senses.label: The just price
senses.summary: Selling above a thing's just value is wrong; price carries a moral standard.
markers: charging more than a thing is worth is a sin

sources.citation: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II–II q. 77

senses.label: Market price and the invisible hand
senses.summary: Prices rise and fall with supply against demand, and self-interested exchange coordinates a whole economy.
markers: prices coordinate production with no one directing it
self-interest produces public benefit through markets

sources.citation: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations (1776), book I ch. 7; book IV ch. 2
sources.note: Natural and market price; the invisible hand.

senses.label: Marginal utility
senses.summary: Value comes from the usefulness of one more unit to the buyer, not from labour or substance.
markers: value depends on the last unit wanted

sources.citation: Jevons, The Theory of Political Economy (1871); Menger, Principles of Economics (1871)

senses.label: Supply-and-demand equilibrium
senses.summary: Price settles where supply and demand curves cross; responsiveness is measured as elasticity.
markers: price is set where supply meets demand
hazards: Bare 'elasticity' is not a term: Darwin's elastic tissue (6 hits).

senses.label: Market power
senses.summary: Firms with few rivals can set prices above competitive levels; market power is analysed and regulated.
markers: a dominant firm can set prices above what competition would allow
hazards: 'Monopoly' is not modern: Aristotle tells of Thales cornering the olive presses (Politics I.11).

sources.citation: Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition (1933); Edward Chamberlin, The Theory of Monopolistic Competition (1933)
